name: Cybersecurity Beyond Phishing
title: Cybersecurity Beyond Phishing
answer: Cybersecurity beyond phishing means treating school security as a set of basic operational protections, vendor obligations, and controls on AI tools, not just as staff awareness training. It matters because a single attack can close schools for days and expose student data, and because vendors and unreviewed AI tools widen that exposure.

sections.body: This idea holds that schools face a constant flow of cyberattacks, including ransomware that locks systems until a payment is made, and that such an attack can halt school operations for days while exposing student information. The problem it solves is the assumption that security is mainly about teaching people to spot phishing emails. The text argues that basic protections make a large difference, naming strong passwords with a second verification step, regular backups kept apart from the main network, and prompt software updates. It also extends the picture to vendors and to AI tools, so security becomes an operational discipline rather than a single training topic.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In day to day school operations, the basic protections are put in place and maintained: strong passwords paired with a second verification step, backups stored separately from the main network, and software updated promptly. Districts also manage vendors by requiring in contracts that they protect data, report breaches quickly, and cooperate with investigations, and by keeping and regularly reviewing a list of every vendor that holds student data. For AI tools, staff are directed away from pasting sensitive information into general chat tools and from connecting tools to district systems without review. The approved tool list described in Chapter 3 serves as both a privacy measure and a security measure, and IT and privacy staff review any tool before it connects to district data. The text does not give grade band variations for this idea.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no study, figure, or formal evidence label for this idea. It states plainly that schools face a steady stream of cyberattacks, that an attack can shut down schools for days and expose student data, and that basic protections make a large difference. These are presented as operational claims rather than as findings from research, so the idea rests on practice and on the book's own account of the risk rather than on cited evidence.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits and risks in the text are that attacks can lock systems until a ransom is paid, can close schools for days, and can expose student data. A breach at a vendor that holds student data can expose information from many districts at once, which is why contracts must require protection, quick breach reporting, and cooperation with investigations. Staff may paste sensitive information into general chat tools or connect tools to district systems without review, so the approved tool list and pre connection review by IT and privacy staff act as controls. The decisions that stay with people are the district's choices about which protections to maintain, which vendors to list and review, and which tools are approved before they touch district data.
